Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Maladaptive Strategies: Substance Use: I drink alcohol, take medication or use drugs, Seeking Conflict: I pick arguments or create drama to distract myself from the trauma, Constant Socialising: I keep myself constantly surrounded by people so I am never alone with my thoughts
  Memory: Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together

Vignette:
Marcus was twelve when the late summer humidity turned the backyard into a heavy, suffocating stage. He remembered the sharp, sweet tang of spilled whiskey cutting through the damp grass, his father’s voice cracking as he stumbled toward the treeline. The screen door had been wrenched from its frame during the shouting match, and when Marcus finally stepped onto the porch, the heavy front door slammed shut behind him, the sound echoing like a split log in the quiet yard. He had come to believe that whenever the woods breathed or a door struck its frame, the past was trying to catch up. What frightened him most was the sudden weight in his chest, a raw, nameless panic that arrived without warning, as if his body held the memory while his mind refused to touch it. Over the years, the event refused to settle into a single picture. When Marcus tried to pull the memory forward, it slipped through his fingers, leaving only the hollow ache and flashes of disconnected moments: a bottle neck resting on the porch steps, the rough texture of bark under his palm, the way his mother’s shoulders tensed but never fully broke. He could not pin it down deliberately, yet the emotions poured through him like tide, complete and unbidden. The sharp, imageless fear and the scattered fragments existed as parallel currents in his daily life, neither yielding to the other. To navigate the days, he packed his calendar with cousins, barbershop regulars, and neighborhood men who needed help with fences or engines, because silence was a room he could no longer enter. When the quiet grew too loud, he would find a crack in the day—a misplaced invoice, a forgotten chore—and let the argument flare, knowing the heat of a dispute would occupy the same space as whatever stirred beneath. He drank before bed, stacked his medication on the nightstand, and kept the radio tuned to talk stations, all of it existing as a steady rhythm rather than a deliberate plan. At seventy-nine, Marcus still clocked in at the regional distribution center, navigating the concrete aisles and metal shelving that hummed with the rhythm of forklifts and freight. The break yard behind the warehouse was overgrown with tall fescue and a scatter of pines, and on days when the wind carried the damp, earthy scent of the woods, his pulse would kick against his ribs. He learned to take the side corridor instead of the main stairwell, avoiding the heavy steel doors that thudded on their hydraulic dampers. The constant murmur of coworkers in the staging area kept his attention anchored, but the distance between him and his former marriage had been a slow, quiet erosion. He had spent decades keeping a crowd between himself and the dark, and when his wife had asked him to stay home on weekends to tend the garden, he had instead driven to the community center, knowing the noise of the crowd would drown out the quiet; the separation had simply been the shape his days took. He had spent years outrunning the quiet, yet at seventy-nine, the pace had grown too heavy. What finally brought him to the clinic was a morning when the warehouse doors opened and the draft carried the sharp tang of spilled grain and damp soil, and he had stood frozen in the loading bay, unable to step forward or back, his breath caught in a throat that no longer knew how to clear it. He was afraid that the old storm would swallow him whole, but he was also hoping, for the first time, that someone might help him learn how to stand still without being consumed.
